title: Museum Frogs Solve a 50-Year Vanishing Mystery
summary:
For nearly 50 years, scientists could not explain why frogs began disappearing from Brazil's Atlantic Forest. Beginning in the 1970s, researchers recorded dramatic declines, but the cause stayed uncertain.

Now researchers have found strong evidence pointing to a deadly fungal disease. The findings, published in Molecular Ecology, come from scientists at the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute and Pennsylvania State University.

The suspected culprit is chytridiomycosis, often called chytrid, caused by the microscopic fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis. Scientists believe the pathogen originated in Asia before spreading around the world during the 1970s and 1980s. But the fungus was not formally identified until 1999, long after amphibian declines had begun.

To solve one such cold case, the team turned to frogs preserved in museum collections. The Smithsonian holds specimens collected by former curator William Ronald Heyer at Brazil's Boracéia Biological Station, where populations crashed between 1979 and 1982 — twice in the 1970s, before the declines, and three times in the 1980s, after them.

The team tested more than 370 preserved amphibians from 17 species. None of the specimens collected before 1979 showed chytrid infection, but more than half of those collected in the 1980s tested positive. The sharp rise suggests the pathogen arrived just as frog populations were collapsing.

There was one surprise. Species that declined most severely showed no detectable infection, while species whose populations stayed relatively stable often carried the fungus. Researchers think some frogs may naturally tolerate the infection, while more vulnerable species may have died so quickly after infection that few infected individuals were ever collected.

While environmental factors could have played a role, Boyette said the findings "most directly implicate the chytrid fungus," showing its arrival coincided with the unexplained disappearances.
why_it_matters: Knowing when and how the fungus spread helps scientists protect the frogs and other amphibians still threatened by the same disease today.

background_read: Chytridiomycosis, or chytrid, is a disease caused by a microscopic fungus that infects the skin of frogs and other amphibians, and it has harmed frog populations in many parts of the world.
Museums keep preserved animal specimens for decades, so scientists can test old specimens to learn when a disease first appeared in a place.
Brazil's Atlantic Forest is a rich habitat where many frog species live, and its frog populations crashed in the 1970s without a proven cause.
